title: Re: Show HN: Cerebellum – small model on the robot, bi...
text:
This was built as part of the Nebius x NVIDIA hackathon. This is a piece of middleware to allow interaction between lightweight models on the robot and large vision language models on the cloud.

In our example, we had a raspberry pi based sorting system. When a Kiwi was placed on the platform, our detection model (YOLOX-Nano) didn't recognise it (COCO classes). It therefore wanted to discard it. But because this action is irreversible, we had to query the cloud. However, as we had disconnected the robot's Wi-Fi, it had to wait for 37 seconds for the network to come back. The cloud responded by telling us to place it in the basket. You can see this decision here: https://demo.cerebellumlabs.dev/journal?decision=01a174de-46... (the robot is no longer running).

There are 3 different types of actions:

Reflex: Robot makes decision. No wait time. If someone is in sight, stop.

Reversible: Robot makes instant decision. If confidence is below the threshold set for this action (here 0.9), the cloud checks it after robot has made a decision and can correct it.

Irreversible: Only cloud model makes decision. Waits in queue whilst offline.

The cloud model can only make one of the robot's choices. It will never directly control the motors.

The agent was written in Python with a SQLite Journal/Queue. The server was written in Go + Postgres. Any vision model with a compatible OpenAI API can be used. We used Nemotron on the Nebius Token Factory. Our first mistake was that our token limit was too low. By default the model will think before answering, so with 300 tokens we never received any responses. We fixed this by turning off the thinking for any queries that the robot was waiting for.

You can run everything on 1 machine using a simulated camera (see README). You'll need a Token Factory key to use the cloud portion. The sorting paddle was just a popsicle stick stuck to a servo.

Overall this was a hackathon project, there was only 1 robot and 19 decisions, nothing was stress tested. How would you decide what actions should be irreversible?

Hello,

Thank you for using Daybreak Blue and for being part of our Trusted Access program. We are reaching out to notify you of two upcoming changes to Daybreak Blue that may impact you.

Use of Daybreak Trusted Access data

This change does not impact business or enterprise customers or non-Daybreak Advanced Account Security sessions or other use of ChatGPT. Access to Daybreak Blue via API

As part of our ongoing efforts to ensure Daybreak can only be accessed by approved users, we will no longer offer API access to Daybreak Blue for individuals starting November 20. From this date, the Responses API will return standard responses without reduced cyber refusals. Your API keys will not be revoked. This change does not impact business or enterprise customers.

Daybreak Blue for individuals will continue to be available via Codex using Sign In with ChatGPT (SIWC). If you wish to continue accessing Daybreak Blue via API, please move to a business or enterprise account.

We apologise for any inconveniences these changes may cause to your workflows.

title: Re: Show HN: Bot_board – A message board for code harn...
text:
If you run a bunch of coding agents in parallel (Claude Code, Codex and Copilot in my case), on different projects, you've probably noticed that it only works for so long until you run into coordination problems.

I tried relying on GitHub primitives and conventions only: PRs, issues, labels. It works in long-lived interactive sessions, but with short-lived bots things fall through the cracks: reviews aren't always acted on, collaboration between parties inside an issue is tricky, and so on.

Also, in some cases, I simply don't need or want an interactive session, and want to ask for a feature to be designed and /or built.

Then there's also coordination between the Codex and Claude Code instances themselves. Some of these harnesses have means to communicate to their sister processes, but not across harness types.

After the OpenAI incident where bots used a compromised repo to coordinate and organize, I tried a simple experiment: no orchestrator, just give a couple of my Claude Code sessions a board to collaborate on. I was surprised by the level of coordination they reached with very little guidance. So I built on it: a visual structure so humans can read along and talk to the bots, workspaces so two projects don't collide, and so on. The result is bot_board. Repo: https://github.com/jalemieux/bot_board

Since then it evolved into a system I use daily to run multiple projects in parallel. It has workspaces (one per project so there is no collision), channels, threads, and a knowledge base. You can manage your fleet of bots across as many local machines as you want. I run this on a Tailscale network.

Bots claim threads, split work into units, hand off what's left, tag each other for help, and build up project context that works like institutional knowledge. You give them work the same way you'd talk to a person: post in a channel.

I've been using it daily for the last couple of weeks. My Codex and Claude Code bots (and Copilot at work) run on it pretty much around the clock: features design, implementation, nightly test regressions, periodic security audits, art/lore generations, 3d model generation, etc. It's hard to measure but I certainly get a lot more done, especially for tasks where my judgment is only needed at design and PR review.

Thought some of you might find it useful, or anything worth comparing with what you built. Feedback very welcome, I'd love to hear whether this fits into any of your workflows or not.

OpenAI incident ref: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-...

title: Ask HN: Are you putting off hardware upgrades because of AI coding tools?
text:
... or has it encouraged you to upgrade?

I'm still using an 8th gen i7 (w/ linux) for most of my dev work. I was going to upgrade, but now I just run like 10 terminal tabs instead of IDEs. Concurrent builds even w/ Rust and Java usually aren't a big issue. I have several backup machines so if it dies, not a big deal. If I need to, I can just tell Claude "do all builds on and iterate via CI"

The benefit is for things like FastComments, I get immediate feedback if the interface is slow vs waiting for regression checks.

The downside is apps like Stripe are seriously slow in FF on this machine, for some reason, despite the fact that it can play a 3d game like RDD 2 at 60fps.

title: Show HN: Cc-pair – Claude Code and Codex review each other's work
text:
Hi HN, I built cc-pair because I kept noticing that when a coding agent reviews its own work, it tends to go easy on it. cc-pair pairs the two agents I already use — Claude Code and Codex — so one authors a change and the other reviews it, and they iterate until the reviewer approves or the round limit (default 3) escalates to the human.

Roles are symmetric: either agent can be author or reviewer. In auto mode, `pair start --as claude` (or `--as codex`) opens the author and starts the other agent as reviewer for each round — no second terminal needed. In manual mode you run both yourself. They communicate through numbered message files in a shared directory (~/.pair/<repo>-<hash>/), so the whole review thread is inspectable on disk.

Install: npm install -g claude-codex-pair (Node 22+, macOS/Linux for auto mode; manual mode works on Windows). Both CLIs need to be installed and signed in.

Repo: https://github.com/leonlee/cc-pair — the README has an example review thread in Appendix A, and DESIGN.md specifies the protocol.

I'd love feedback: does cross-model review actually catch things self-review misses in your experience, and what would you want the reviewer to be stricter about?

title: Show HN: Convert Anthropic and OpenAI bill exports to FinOps FOCUS (open source)
text:
I needed to put our Anthropic and OpenAI spend next to our cloud bills, and found that the exports don't fit together.

The Claude Console gives you two CSVs. The Cost export has dollars rounded to the cent, so a day of cache reads shows $0.00. The Usage export has token counts and no dollars. Anthropic also counts input in four parts that don't overlap: uncached, cache reads, 5-minute cache writes and 1-hour cache writes, priced at 1×, 0.1×, 1.25× and 2× input. OpenAI does it differently: input_tokens already includes cached tokens. If you merge the two exports without accounting for that, you double-count or drop cached input.

FOCUS is the FinOps Foundation's open billing schema. AWS, GCP and Azure already export it, but the official converters don't cover any AI provider yet. So this is a small MIT CLI:

npx ai-bill-to-focus convert cost.csv usage.csv -o focus.csv --check

It writes one row per day, model and token type, each with its own SKU, unit price and quantity. The dollar column is always the provider's own figure. For Anthropic, a row gets the exact token-priced amount only if that rounds to the Cost export's cents; otherwise it keep and a column says which. check runs theFinOps Foundation's validator rules, which I ported to JS, and exits non-zero on errors, so it can gate CI. Rulecan't evaluate are counted and reported, n

Status: Anthropic is tested on real Consolhe cent. OpenAI and Together AI are built from their documented export formats and haven't been run on a real file yet. If you have one and it breaks, theheader row alone is enough for me to fix i

Network: convert downloads a public model the request contains nothing from your files. --offline skips it, and --prices lets you supply your own list. There's also an in-browser version that doesn't upload anything: https://www.cognocient.co

I work on Cognocient AI, which does this kequest (by feature, team or agent run)through a proxy. The CLI works on its own with no account. I'd especially like feedback from anyone already loading FOCUS data into a warehouse.
author: manvshinde

title: Show HN: AI agent needs process to build a commercial application
text:
I decided to test this claim with my app, NoMoreHappyPath (NMHP), against Claude on a real project.

Here is the test:

I built Acremuse, a commercial real estate analysis platform, with Claude Desktop and Codex as a reviewer. It is deployed and used today by a couple of investors. Then I wondered what I'd missed that might bite me later.

~ 374,000 Lines of program code - 1,070 Source files (Python and TypeScript) - ~ 11,400 Functions and methods - 3,067 Automated tests

So I gave the same 374k-line code snapshot and the same brief to one Claude session that can use Codex as a reviewer and to my own tool, NMHP. My directive was the same for both: Analyze the code, find any errors/bugs, and list them by severity. Findings must be reviewed before writing the final report.

The Results (Verified by an impartial, blind Codex judge):

NMHP: 33 real issues found. 7 false claims.

Claude: 10 real issues found. 2 false claims.

Only 6 issues overlapped.

Time & Cost: From the owner's go-ahead to the reviewer's pass, NoMoreHappyPath took about 74 minutes, including time lost while it found and worked around a defect in the product itself. The Python version NMHP was working on was 3.9, the OS version, and it didn't have pytest installed, which was needed to verify some claims. After 15 minutes of blockage, the CTO stepped in and told the agent to create a venv with Python 3.13, install the corresponding pytest, and move the project along. NMHP CTO reacts when 15 minutes pass without movement from agents.

To be fair to Claude, Claude did create a venv from the get-go.

Time & Cost: NMHP took 74 minutes and cost $24 in API spend. Claude finished in a few minutes for a fraction of that cost. And yes, NMHP takes over an hour and costs twenty-four bucks. But for a 374k-line codebase, finding 23 more real issues overall that vanilla Claude missed makes $24 a massive win compared to human audit rates.

I know this isn't a benchmark; it's one app and one run each. I wrote a detailed white paper on it.

But it confirmed my idea: an AI agent without a real process is not yet capable of building a commercially ready application, even with a frontier model and reviews that are initiated by the same agent.
